reference.source: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine / ESC & ACC-AHA guidelines
clinicalPearls: SVT is a broad term for regular, usually narrow-complex tachycardias originating at or above the atrioventricular node, most commonly AV nodal reentrant tachycardia and AV reentrant tachycardia using an accessory pathway
Typical presentation is abrupt-onset, regular palpitations with sudden termination, often with lightheadedness, chest discomfort, or breathlessness
The QRS is usually narrow unless there is aberrant conduction or a pre-existing bundle branch block, when it can mimic ventricular tachycardia
Vagal manoeuvres are the first-line acute intervention to interrupt reentry through the AV node
When vagal manoeuvres fail in a stable patient, an AV nodal blocking agent given under monitoring is the usual next step
Synchronised cardioversion is indicated when the patient is haemodynamically unstable
Catheter ablation offers a high cure rate for recurrent AVNRT and AVRT and is a definitive long-term option
A regular narrow-complex tachycardia should be distinguished from atrial flutter and atrial fibrillation, which have different management
reference.pathophysiology: Most paroxysmal SVT is caused by reentry. In AV nodal reentrant tachycardia a functional circuit forms within or near the AV node using fast and slow pathways. In AV reentrant tachycardia the circuit incorporates an accessory pathway connecting atrium and ventricle, as in Wolff-Parkinson-White. Atrial tachycardias instead arise from an ectopic atrial focus with enhanced automaticity or microreentry. In reentrant mechanisms a premature beat finds one limb refractory and conducts down the other, then returns retrogradely, establishing a self-sustaining loop that the AV node often participates in, which is why AV nodal blockade frequently terminates the arrhythmia.
additionalInvestigations: 12-lead ECG during tachycardia and in sinus rhythm to characterise the mechanism and detect pre-excitation
Continuous rhythm monitoring or ambulatory ECG for paroxysmal episodes
Electrolyte and thyroid function assessment to identify reversible triggers
Echocardiography to exclude structural heart disease
Electrophysiology study to define the circuit when ablation is considered
redFlags: Haemodynamic instability with hypotension, ischaemic chest pain, pulmonary oedema, or reduced consciousness, requiring urgent synchronised cardioversion
Wide-complex tachycardia that cannot be confidently distinguished from ventricular tachycardia, which should be treated as VT until proven otherwise
Pre-excited tachycardia where AV nodal blocking drugs may be hazardous
reference.prognosis: Most forms of SVT are not life-threatening and carry an excellent prognosis, with catheter ablation curing the majority of reentrant cases; prognosis worsens when SVT complicates structural heart disease or occurs as pre-excited tachycardia with a risk of rapid ventricular rates.
pitfalls: Giving AV nodal blocking drugs in a pre-excited tachycardia, which can accelerate ventricular response
Misdiagnosing a wide-complex tachycardia as SVT with aberrancy when it is actually ventricular tachycardia
Delaying cardioversion in an unstable patient while attempting pharmacological control
Overlooking reversible precipitants such as stimulants, thyroid disease, or electrolyte disturbance
management: Terminate acute stable episodes first with vagal manoeuvres to interrupt reentry through the AV node
Give an AV nodal blocking agent such as adenosine under continuous monitoring when vagal manoeuvres fail, using verapamil, diltiazem or a beta-blocker as alternatives
Perform immediate synchronised cardioversion when the patient is haemodynamically unstable
Offer catheter ablation as curative definitive treatment for recurrent reentrant SVT
Use long-term beta-blockers or calcium-channel blockers for prevention when ablation is declined or unsuitable
Avoid AV nodal blocking drugs in pre-excited atrial fibrillation associated with an accessory pathway
Identify and correct reversible triggers such as electrolyte disturbance, thyroid dysfunction and stimulants, and refer to cardiology electrophysiology
